label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**The view from the other side of the morning**

I did my last night shift on Saturday. 21:00 to 07:30, majors, the same as hundreds of others. Nobody made a fuss, because I asked them not to, and because it was a Saturday in November and there wasn't time anyway. From Monday I'm on the days-only rota. My knees have been filing complaints for a while, my sleep has been a sort of rumour for longer than that, and in the summer my GP looked at my blood pressure readings and said, quite kindly, that it was not a joke anymore. So that was that.

I've tried to write this post about five times since spring. It kept turning into a eulogy, as if someone had died, or into a rant about the NHS, and I've written enough of those. I don't want either. I want to be honest about what fourteen years of nights gave me and what they cost, and I want to do it before it all goes soft-focus in my memory.

My first night was as an SHO in 2012. I was terrified in the specific way you only are at 28, when you're sure everyone can tell you don't know what you're doing and you're sure they're right. That first winter I finished a shift, walked out to the car park at the Infirmary, got in the car and cried, because I couldn't remember whether I'd given a patient their second dose. I sat there with the engine off, going back through the night in my head, building and knocking down the same timeline over and over. I had given it. I'd written it down. I knew I had. But you don't trust anything at 8am after your first proper run of nights, least of all yourself. I can still see the frost on the windscreen, thick enough that I had to wait for it to clear before I could leave. I've thought about that frost a lot over the years. I never managed to make the fear go away completely, but I did learn to carry it differently.

People assume nights are all adrenaline: the resus bay at 2am, the trauma call, the dramatic stuff off the telly. There's some of that. But mostly, honestly, nights are about staying kind at 5am when you've got nothing left. That's the hardest part of the job and I don't think anyone warns you about it. Being good in a crisis is easy enough, because the crisis carries you. The test comes in the flat grey hours after. The fourth person in a row who has waited six hours and is angry about it, and has every right to be. The relative who needs the same thing explained a third time because they couldn't take it in the first two. You do it gently because that's the job, and because you'd want someone to do it gently for you. Some nights I managed it. Some nights I didn't, and I drove home thinking about the ones where I'd been short with someone, and promised myself I'd do better. I don't think that promise ever quite stops.

Nights are where the department is most itself. I've believed that for years and I'll keep saying it. There are fewer managers about, fewer meetings, fewer people who need to be seen doing something. What's left is the people actually doing the work, and a kind of honesty you don't get in daylight. People say what they mean at 3am. They're also kinder, in a way that's hard to explain if you haven't worked a night shift. Somebody notices you haven't sat down for six hours and puts a cup of tea at your elbow without saying anything. Somebody takes the patient you were dreading. It isn't sentimental. People just know that tonight it's them and tomorrow it might be you.

Which brings me to the toast.

At around 4am, someone always makes toast in the staff room. Always. In fourteen years I've never once seen who starts it. You go in to refill your water bottle and there's a plate of it on the side, buttered, sometimes with jam if it's been a good week, and someone's already halfway through a slice. Ask who made it and everyone looks blank. Nobody admits to starting it. I've accused at least three different consultants and a porter. I have my suspicions about one particular HCA. I'm not going to name them. But on some of the worst nights I've worked, that toast was the thing that got me through to 7:30. It isn't really about food. It tells you someone thought about the rest of us.

There's an old gentleman I still think about, from last winter. I won't say much, because his story belongs to him. It was about 3am and quiet in the way the department occasionally is, the quiet you're superstitious about mentioning. I was checking on him, and he reached out and held my hand, looked at it for a while, and told me I had his daughter's hands. That was all. He went home three days later. I don't know what he saw in my hands. Mostly they're dry from hand gel and there's a scar on one knuckle from a car door in 2017. But I've thought about him a lot since then, and I think of him whenever someone asks me why I stayed on nights so long. That kind of moment happens in daylight too, I'm sure. It just seemed to happen to me more at 3am, when people have stopped performing for each other.

Nights also took things from me, and I'd be lying if I left that out. My sleep has never been right. My body seems to have lost track of what time it is somewhere around 2015 and never quite found it again. Then there are the things I missed. I watched both my nieces' naming ceremonies over video, propped on the kitchen counter at home, still in scrubs, on the far side of the world from Bangalore and from the right time of day. My sister never once complained. Not once, through all of it. She would send photos afterwards and ask how my shift went. I'm not sure she knows how much that meant to me, so I'm putting it here, where she'll read it. Thank you, akka. I owe you more than I can write.

And then there's Folasade. She's our charge nurse on nights and she's done twenty-two years of them. Twenty-two. She still beats me up the stairs every time, and she doesn't let me forget it. If the department really is most itself at night, then a good part of what it is, is her. She knows which junior doctor is about to cry before they do. She knows which patient is going to go off before the obs show it. She has a look that can silence an entire corridor and another look that tells you you're doing fine, and she uses both exactly when they're needed. When I told her I was moving to days, she said, "About time," and then she didn't speak to me for the rest of the shift, which from Folasade is about as close to sentiment as it gets.

Driving home on Sunday morning I went down the London Road with the sun coming up and the shipping forecast on catch-up, which is a habit I've never been able to explain to anyone who hasn't done nights. Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. The light was that particular low orange you only get in November, coming in sideways over the rooftops. Somewhere around the station it hit me that I wouldn't see that light from this side again. I'll see sunrises, obviously. But I won't be seeing them at the end of something, tired and wrung out and a bit raw, with the night still on me. I'll be seeing them at the start of the day like everybody else.

What I keep coming back to is that I'm relieved. Really relieved. I'm looking forward to sleeping when it's dark, and I'd quite like my blood pressure to stop being a topic of conversation. But I also feel like a traitor for feeling that way. I feel like I've left a room full of people I love and they're all still in there, at 4am, making toast, looking after each other, and I've just walked out. I know that isn't fair to myself. People move on to other things all the time and it's fine. Folasade would tell me to stop being dramatic. But knowing that doesn't make the feeling go away, and I'd rather be honest about it here than pretend otherwise.

So, days. I'll learn the new rhythm. I'll find out who makes the tea on the day side, if anyone does. I'll probably be insufferable for a while about how much better nights were. Forgive me in advance.

But this post isn't really about me. I'll leave you with this. Tonight, and tomorrow night, and every night after, there will be people in that department doing the hardest version of the job in the quietest hours. Folasade will be there, running up the stairs ahead of whoever is new. And at around 4am, somebody will go into the staff room and quietly put the toaster on, and nobody will ever admit it was them.

---

A couple of quick notes. I've used "akka" for your sister, since you mentioned Bangalore, but swap it for whatever you actually call her (or just her name). I made up small details like the knuckle scar, the 2017 car door and Folasade's "About time", so change or cut anything that isn't true. It comes to roughly 1,600 words.

reasons: It says the doctor watched both naming ceremonies rather than missing them, and adds that the elderly gentleman looked at the doctor's hand for a while.
